questions.title: Average number of people per household in the United States
questions.hint: Household size depends on how many children people have, when young adults leave home, and how long older people live on their own.
questions.explanation: It fell to 2.50 in 2025, from 3.33 in 1955.

questions.title: Share of electricity from nuclear power in the United States
questions.hint: Very few new US reactors were started after the Three Mile Island accident in 1979.
questions.explanation: It barely moved: 21% in 2001 and 17% in 2025.

questions.title: Death rate from stroke in the United States
questions.hint: High blood pressure is the main cause of strokes, and treating it became routine only in the second half of the century.
questions.explanation: It fell to 38 in 2015, from 167 in 1945. Age-adjusted to the 2000 US population. How causes are coded changed with each revision of the international classification (1949, 1958, 1968, 1979, 1999), which moves some deaths between causes.

source.attribution: US CDC, National Center for Health Statistics

questions.title: Average age of US senators at the start of each Congress
questions.hint: A young republic, then incumbents who keep winning re-election, with the occasional wave election that sweeps in a fresh class.
questions.explanation: It went from 56.9 in 1933 to a low of 53.5 in 1983, then ended at 63.5 in 2023. The 1978-80 wave of newcomers dropped the average to 52.3 in 1981, its lowest since the 1870s; it has climbed since to the oldest ever. Each point is the Senate on the day a new Congress first met.

questions.title: Federal spending as a share of GDP in the United States
questions.unitLabel: federal outlays, % of GDP, fiscal years
questions.hint: Wars and recessions push spending up relative to the economy; programs like Social Security and Medicare add to it steadily.
questions.explanation: It went from 16.7% in 1965 to a high of 30.5% in 2020, then ended at 23.1% in 2025. Federal fiscal years: until 1976 they ended in June, since 1977 in September. Federal spending only, not state and local.

source.attribution: US Office of Management and Budget
